reason: The provided sources contain ample verified facts to support a surprising 45-second script about the Coma Cluster and the discovery of dark matter.
story: In 1933, Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky pointed his telescope at the Coma Cluster, a massive cosmic city containing over a thousand galaxies located 321 million light years away. When Zwicky calculated how fast these galaxies were moving, he stumbled upon a startling mathematical crisis. Based on the visible light and mass of the stars, the cluster should have flown apart instantly; its gravity was far too weak to hold it together. Yet, the galaxies were speeding along wildly while remaining tightly bound. To solve this impossible riddle, Zwicky proposed a radical hypothesis: an invisible, massive substance he called dunkle Materie—dark matter—must be filling the void, outweighing visible stars by up to ninety percent and acting as an invisible gravitational glue. Though astronomers largely ignored him for decades, Zwicky had just discovered that everything we can actually see in the universe is merely a tiny fraction of reality.
angle: In 1933, astronomer Fritz Zwicky discovered that a massive city of galaxies was moving so fast it should have flown apart, proving that 90% of the universe is made of invisible 'dark matter' we still cannot touch.

claims.claim: The Coma Cluster contains over 1,000 identified galaxies.
The Coma Cluster's mean distance from Earth is 321 million light years (99 Mpc).
In 1933, Fritz Zwicky studied the Coma Cluster and used the virial theorem to discover a gravitational anomaly.
Zwicky found that the galaxies were moving too fast for the cluster to be bound together by visible matter alone.
Zwicky coined or used the term "dunkle Materie" (dark matter) to explain the missing mass.
About 90% of the mass of the Coma cluster is believed to be in the form of dark matter.
Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer who worked at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
The Coma Cluster is located in the constellation Coma Berenices.
Zwicky's 1933 paper on the redshift of extragalactic nebulae was published in Helvetica Physica Acta.
Zwicky published a follow-up paper on galaxy clusters and mass-to-light ratios in the Astrophysical Journal in 1937.
The idea of dark matter was not widely accepted by the astronomical community for another fifty years.

disputed: Whether Zwicky's 1933 paper used exactly seven galaxies or eight galaxies or a count of 800 for his initial calculations (different sources cite different numbers of galaxies analyzed in his initial velocity dispersion steps; script should focus generally on the cluster's overall velocity dispersion and counts of over a thousand identified members).
